name: Lote
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

new_statements.quote: Stress is penultimate on isolated words and noun phrases and is phonetically realised by loudness and pitch. The rhythm of spoken Lote is based on syllable-timed intonation. Questions end on a high + low falling tone contour. Statements and commands end on a low tone. There is no contrastive length. However, lengthened consonants are phonetically heard in multi-syllabic words when two identical consonants meet at a syllable boundary. pit.te ['pit:e] 'rain' (dialectal variant pilte); chan.na.nga [xa'n:aŋa] 'fooling'

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog penultimate stress (penultimate) matches the stated penultimate stress exactly; the sketch adds the domain note (isolated words and noun phrases) and the phonetic correlates (loudness and pitch), and states no contrastive length.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a word spoken in isolation, and on the penultimate syllable of a noun phrase (i.e. the domain is the phrase when words are grouped); it is realised by loudness and pitch. No contrastive vowel or consonant length; rhythm is syllable-timed; sentence-final intonation contours distinguish questions from statements.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The only nuance is that the domain is 'isolated words and noun phrases', so inside a noun phrase the word-level penult may not carry the phrase stress; the two transcribed examples ['pit:e] and [xa'n:aŋa] show penultimate stress. The chapter is 'a revised version of Pearson and Pearson (1997)' (Lote Phonology Essentials, unpublished ms).
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar sketch (sec. 1.3, p. 2-3) distinguishes three Lote dialects (beach, inland, eastern) differing 'mostly in the area of intonation and a number of vocabulary items'; the authors worked chiefly with Tavolo village speakers (acknowledgements) plus Pilematana, Meletong, Uvol, Ruach and Maso. The stress statement is given for Lote generally, not for one dialect. Lote = Uvol [uvl]; Ross 1988 classifies it as Western Oceanic, North New Guinea, Ngero-Vitiaz, Mengen.

audit.reasoning: The classification (penultimate, fixed-dominant) rests on the standard and only published description of Lote, a 2008 SIL reference-style grammar sketch by a fieldworker with 20+ years in the community, and the deciding sentence is confirmed verbatim at sec. 2.4 p. 14 in a copy we hold (now also filed in our files); same-page phonetic transcriptions independently show penultimate stress. The record's grade/quote/cite/loc fields are empty even though the source text is verified, so the strength of the evidence should be set to primary-source-verified with locator 'sec. 2.4, p. 14'. The statement is categorical with no listed exceptions, so 'fixed' (strict) would also be defensible, but a two-sentence sketch statement restricted to 'isolated words and noun phrases' is a reasonable basis for keeping dominant rather than strict; no reclassification is warranted on present evidence.
